title: Drawing the boundary
objectives: Read a classifier's decision boundary and move its threshold
Choose a threshold from the costs of the two errors
Compare a flexible and a linear boundary on test data

screens.prose: The bank now uses two features: leverage and interest cover. Each dot is one of the 100 most recent loans; orange ones defaulted. The model refuses a loan when its default probability is at least the threshold $t$.

derive.caption: $t$ = {{fixed(t, 2)}}: refuse {{params.flag[round(t*20)]}} of 100 loans, catching {{params.tp[round(t*20)]}} of the 28 defaults

screens.question: Slide $t$ from 0.5 down to 0.3. What changes?

options.text: The line slides parallel towards safer loans: more loans refused, more defaults caught, more good loans refused too
The line tilts to a new angle
options.why: You expected the threshold to change the slope. Only the level the line sits at changes, so it moves parallel.

options.text: Fewer loans are refused
options.why: A lower threshold refuses loans at a lower probability, so more loans cross it: 17 at 0.5, 28 at 0.3.

options.text: Only defaulted loans join the refused side
options.why: Six more defaults are caught at 0.3, but five more good loans are refused as well, 7 instead of 2.

hints.text: Watch the caption as well as the line.
Compare the line's angle at 0.5 and at 0.3.
At 0.3 the line has moved parallel, down and left. 28 loans are refused instead of 17, and 21 defaults are caught instead of 15.

feedback.correct: Lowering $t$ moves the line parallel: more refusals, more defaults caught, more good loans lost.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the line and the caption at 0.5 and at 0.3.

explain.text: At 0.5 the bank refuses 17 loans and catches 15 defaults; at 0.3 it refuses 28 and catches 21. The 11 extra refusals include 5 loans that would have repaid. The line never turns, it only slides.

screens.prose: Every loan on the line gets the same probability, $t$. The line is the **decision boundary**: refuse on one side, lend on the other. The model is $z = -1.966 + 0.602\,\text{lev} - 0.534\,\text{cover}$, so the boundary is where $z = \ln\dfrac{t}{1-t}$.
screens.question: At $t = 0.3$, what value of the log-odds $z$ does the boundary sit at?

hints.text: The line is where $p = t$. Turn $t$ into log-odds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the odds $t/(1-t)$, then take the natural log.

byKey.p: 0.3 is the probability on the line. The model's left-hand side is in log-odds.
byKey.lnp: You took $\ln 0.3$. The log-odds are the log of $0.3/0.7$.
byKey.sign: A threshold below 0.5 sits at negative log-odds.

explain.text: On the boundary $-1.966 + 0.602\,\text{lev} - 0.534\,\text{cover} = -0.847$, one straight line. Changing $t$ changes only the right-hand side, which is why the line slid without turning.

screens.prose: Each threshold splits the 100 recent loans four ways. 28 of them defaulted and 72 repaid. Use the slider to check the first two columns.

derive.caption: $t$ = {{fixed(t, 2)}}: refuse {{params.flag[round(t*20)]}} of 100 loans, catching {{params.tp[round(t*20)]}} of the 28 defaults

screens.question: Fill in the missing counts.

hints.text: Every refused loan either defaulted or would have repaid.
Refused but would repay = refused − refused and defaulted. Lent and defaulted = 28 − refused and defaulted.

feedback.correct: Raising $t$ cuts false alarms from 7 to 0 and lets missed defaults grow from 7 to 20.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Refused splits into defaulted and would repay; the 28 defaults split into refused and lent.

byKey.r0c3: Refused 28, of which 21 defaulted: $28 - 21 = 7$ would have repaid.
byKey.r0c4: 21 of the 28 defaults were refused, so $28 - 21 = 7$ were lent to.
byKey.r1c3: Refused 17, of which 15 defaulted: 2 would have repaid.
byKey.r1c4: 15 of the 28 defaults were refused, so 13 were lent to.
byKey.r2c3: All 8 refused loans defaulted, so none would have repaid.
byKey.r2c4: 8 of the 28 defaults were refused, so 20 were lent to.

explain.text: **True positives** were refused and defaulted; **false positives** were refused but would repay. **False negatives** were lent to and defaulted; the rest are **true negatives**. Moving $t$ up trades false positives for false negatives, and no threshold removes both.

screens.prose: A missed default costs the bank £50,000. Refusing a loan that would have repaid costs £2,000 of lost business. $t = 0$ refuses every loan; $t = 1$ refuses none.
screens.question: Fill in the total cost over the 100 loans at each threshold, in £.

hints.text: Cost = false alarms × £2,000 + missed defaults × £50,000.
At $t = 0$ there are no missed defaults, only 72 false alarms.

feedback.correct: Refusing everyone, £144,000, is the cheapest of the five.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each column by its cost and add.

byKey.r0c3: 72 good loans refused at £2,000 each is £144,000; no default slips through.
byKey.r4c3: Lending to all 100 misses all 28 defaults: £1,400,000.

explain.text: With misses 25 times dearer than false alarms, the usual 0.5 costs £654,000 and refusing everyone costs £144,000. Refusing everyone is a bad bet, but 0.5 is worse. The best threshold must sit far below 0.3.

screens.prose: Where should the threshold sit? Take one loan whose model probability of default is $p$, and compare the expected cost of each decision.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Lend: expected cost $p \times \text{£}50{,}000$, the chance it defaults times the loss
Refuse: expected cost $(1 - p) \times \text{£}2{,}000$, the chance it repays times the lost business
Refuse when $(1 - p) \times 2{,}000 < p \times 50{,}000$: take the cheaper decision
$p > \dfrac{2{,}000}{2{,}000 + 50{,}000} = 0.038$: collect the $p$ terms on one side

hints.text: Write down the two expected costs first.
Refusing is better when its expected cost is smaller.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. State both expected costs, compare them, then solve for $p$.

byKey.cmp: The comparison needs both expected costs above it.
byKey.solve: Solving for $p$ is the last step.

explain.text: In general, refuse when $p > \dfrac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}$; with equal costs that is 0.5. On our test loans $t = 0.04$ costs £94,000, against £654,000 at 0.5. The rule trusts $p$ to be a real probability, which lesson 13 checks.

screens.prose: An analyst tries every threshold from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.01 on the 100 test loans. The cheapest is $t = 0.15$, costing £92,000. Chosen on the 300 training loans instead, the best is $t = 0.04$; on the test loans it costs £94,000.
screens.question: Which cost should the bank expect on next year's loans?

options.why: You took the threshold that looked best on the test loans. Choosing it there used the test set for fitting, so its cost is flattering.

options.text: £94,000, with $t = 0.04$ chosen on training loans
£654,000, with the standard $t = 0.5$
options.why: 0.5 is a convention, not a law. With these costs it is the worst choice of the three.

options.text: It does not matter: the two differ by only £2,000
options.why: The gap is small here, but the habit is not. Scan 101 thresholds on a small test set and the winner is lucky by construction.

hints.text: Which threshold was chosen without looking at the test loans?
A test set gives an honest score only for a model that never saw it. Choosing $t$ is part of fitting.
Choose $t$ on training data, then score it once on test: £94,000.

feedback.correct: Choose $t$ on training data and score it once on test.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which figure was produced without looking at the test loans.

byKey.test: You took the threshold that looked best on the test loans. Choosing it there used the test set for fitting, so its cost is flattering.

explain.text: The threshold is a parameter of the model, so it must be fitted on training data. The training choice, 0.04, sits next to the formula's 0.038. A test score after tuning on the test set is a training score in disguise.

screens.prose: In level 1 you met $k$-nearest neighbours. With $k = 1$ it copies the label of the closest training loan. Its boundary (yellow) wraps round every training loan; logistic regression's is the straight line. The dots are the 300 training loans.

state.caption: Yellow: the $k = 1$ boundary. Green: logistic regression at $t = 0.5$.

screens.question: On the 100 test loans, which classifier makes fewer mistakes?

options.text: Logistic regression: 15 mistakes against 25
$k$-NN: it makes no mistakes on the training loans
options.why: Training error lies, as in lesson 2. With $k = 1$ every training loan is its own nearest neighbour, so training error is 0 by construction.

options.text: $k$-NN: a wiggly boundary can fit any shape
options.why: Flexibility pays only when the true boundary is wiggly. Here it chases noise in the training loans and makes 25 test mistakes.

options.text: They tie, because both were fitted to the same loans
options.why: Same data, different flexibility. The straight line misses 15 test loans; $k = 1$ misses 25.

hints.text: Think about lesson 2 before you trust the yellow boundary.
$k = 1$ has no training errors at all. What does that say about its variance?
On the test loans logistic regression at 0.5 makes 15 mistakes and $k = 1$ makes 25.

feedback.correct: The straight line wins on new loans: 15 mistakes against 25.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge each boundary on loans it has not seen.

byKey.knn0: Training error lies, as in lesson 2. With $k = 1$ every training loan is its own nearest neighbour, so training error is 0 by construction.

explain.text: The $k = 1$ boundary has high variance: move one training loan and it changes. The logistic line has two slopes to fit and stays put. A squared feature such as $\text{lev}^2$ (lesson 6) would bend the line for one extra coefficient.

screens.prose: A signal gives a calibrated probability $p$ that a trade wins. A winner makes £200; a loser costs £300. The desk trades only when the expected profit is positive.
screens.question: Above what probability should the signal fire?

hints.text: Write the expected profit of one trade.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the expected profit $200p - 300(1-p)$ above 0 and solve.

byKey.swap: You swapped the two amounts. The threshold is the loss over the total, $300/500$.
byKey.half: 0.5 balances equal stakes. A loser costs more than a winner makes, so you need to win more often.

explain.text: The signal must fire only above 0.6, because each loss is bigger than each win. It is the bank's rule again with a missed trade costing nothing: $t = \text{loss}/(\text{win} + \text{loss})$.

ideas: The decision boundary is where $p = t$. For logistic regression on two features it is a straight line, and moving $t$ slides it parallel.
Raising $t$ trades false positives for false negatives; refuse when $p > c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$.
The threshold is part of the model: choose it on training data and score it once on test.

formula.name: Cost threshold
formula.note: Equal costs give 0.5; a dear miss pushes it down.

summary.trap: Treating 0.5 as a law, or tuning the threshold on the test set and reporting that cost.

quiz.prose: A risk alert fires when the model's probability of a limit breach exceeds $t$. A false alarm costs £150 of a trader's time; a missed breach costs £6,000.
quiz.question: Which threshold minimises the expected cost? Give 3 decimal places.

byKey.swap: You put the miss in the numerator. The alert fires above the false-alarm cost over the total.
byKey.ratio: $150/6{,}000 = 0.025$ divides by the miss cost alone. The denominator is the sum of both costs.

explain.text: $t = 150/(150 + 6{,}000) = 0.024$. A missed breach is 40 times dearer than a false alarm, so the alert fires at the faintest hint.

quiz.prose: We add $\text{lev}^2$ to the loan model: $z = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{lev} + \beta_2\,\text{cover} + \beta_3\,\text{lev}^2$.
quiz.question: What shape is the decision boundary in the leverage–cover plane?

options.text: A parabola: cover on the boundary is a quadratic in leverage
Still a straight line: the model is still linear
options.why: It is linear in the coefficients, not in leverage. On the boundary, cover $= (\ln\frac{t}{1-t} - \beta_0 - \beta_1\text{lev} - \beta_3\text{lev}^2)/\beta_2$.

options.text: A circle round the riskiest loans
options.why: A circle would need $\text{cover}^2$ as well, with matching coefficients.

options.text: A wiggly curve like $k$-NN's
options.why: One squared term bends the line once. $k$-NN's boundary wraps round individual loans.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $z = \ln\frac{t}{1-t}$ for cover.

explain.text: Solving for cover gives a quadratic in leverage, so the boundary is a parabola. Feature making, as in lesson 6, bends a linear model's boundary while it stays linear in its coefficients.

quiz.prose: On the 100 test loans, 28 defaulted. Set the threshold to $t = 1$.
quiz.question: What does the bank do, and what does it cost at £50,000 a missed default?

options.text: It lends to all 100 loans and loses £1,400,000
It refuses all 100 loans and loses £144,000
options.why: That is $t = 0$. At $t = 1$ no probability reaches the threshold, so nothing is refused.

options.text: It refuses only loans it is sure of, so it costs nothing
options.why: No loan scores 1, so none is refused. All 28 defaults are lent to.

options.text: It behaves like $t = 0.5$
options.why: Each threshold is a different rule. At 1 the boundary has left the chart.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which loans have a probability of at least 1.

explain.text: No loan scores 1, so all are lent to and all 28 defaults cost £50,000: £1,400,000. The two edges, $t = 0$ and $t = 1$, are the 'always refuse' and 'always lend' rules.

quiz.prose: A colleague says a classifier should always use $t = 0.5$, because there the model is 'more sure than not'.
quiz.question: When is 0.5 the threshold with the lowest expected cost?

options.text: When a false positive and a false negative cost the same
When the classes are balanced
options.why: Class balance changes how many errors of each kind you make. The threshold depends on what each error costs.

options.text: Always: probabilities above 0.5 mean 'yes'
options.why: The decision depends on costs as well. With a miss 25 times dearer, the bank refuses above 0.038.

options.text: Never

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put equal costs into $c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$.

explain.text: With $c_{FP} = c_{FN}$ the cost threshold $c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$ is exactly 0.5. Any other pair of costs moves it.
